'''''Myriophyllum spicatum''''' ('''Eurasian watermilfoil'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=MYSP2|taxon=Myriophyllum spicatum|access-date=15 July 2015}}</ref> or '''spiked water-milfoil''') is a submerged [[perennial]] [[aquatic plant]] which grows in still or slow-moving water. Eurasian watermilfoil is native to [[Europe]], [[Asia]], and [[North Africa]], but has a wide geographic and climatic distribution among some 57 countries, extending from northern [[Canada]] to [[South Africa]].<ref name="cabi">{{cite web |title=''Myriophyllum spicatum'' (spiked watermilfoil) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/34941 |publisher=CABI |access-date=4 March 2019 |date=6 November 2018}}</ref> It is considered to be a highly [[invasive species]].<ref name=cabi/>

==Description==
Eurasian watermilfoil has slender stems up to {{convert|250|cm|ft}} long.<ref name=cabi/> The submerged [[leaf|leaves]] (usually between 15–35 mm long) are borne in pinnate whorls of four, with numerous thread-like leaflets roughly 4–13 mm long. Plants are [[monoecious]] with [[flower]]s produced in the leaf axils (male above, female below) on a spike 5–15 cm long held vertically above the water surface, each flower is inconspicuous, orange-red, 4–6 mm long. Eurasian watermilfoil has 12–21 pairs of leaflets while northern watermilfoil ''M. sibiricum'' only has 5–9 pairs. The two can hybridize and the resulting hybrid plants can cause taxonomic confusion as leaf characters are intermediate and can overlap with parent species.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Moody|first=M. L.|author2=Les, D. H.|journal=Biological Invasions|year=2007|volume=9|pages=559–570|doi=10.1007/s10530-006-9058-9|title=Geographic distribution and genotypic composition of invasive hybrid watermilfoil (Myriophyllum spicatum × M. sibiricum) populations in North America|issue=5|bibcode=2007BiInv...9..559M |s2cid=101649}}</ref>

==Chemistry==
''Myriophyllum spicatum'' produces [[ellagic acid|ellagic]], [[gallic acid|gallic]] and [[pyrogallic acid]]s and (+)-[[catechin]], allelopathic polyphenols inhibiting the growth of blue-green alga ''[[Microcystis aeruginosa]]''.<ref name="Nakai">Myriophyllum spicatum-released allelopathic polyphenols inhibiting growth of blue-greenalgaeMicrocystis aeruginosa. Satoshi Nakai, Yutaka Inoue, Masaaki Hosomi and Akihiko Murakami, Water Research, Volume 34, Issue 11, 1 August 2000, Pages 3026–3032, {{doi|10.1016/S0043-1354(00)00039-7}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Myriophyllum spicatum'' is found in disperse regions of [[North America]], [[Europe]], [[Asia]], [[Australia (continent)|Australia]], and [[Africa]].<ref name=cabi/>

==Invasive species==
===Introduced areas===
''Myriophyllum spicatum'' was likely first introduced to [[North America]] in the 1940s<ref>{{cite journal|last=Couch|first=R.|author2=Nelson, E.|title=''Myriophyllum spicatum'' in North America|journal=Proceedings of the First International Symposium on Watermilfoil (Myriophyllum Spicatum) and Related Haloragaceae Species|year=1985|pages=8–18}}</ref> where it has become an [[invasive species]] in some areas. By the mid 1970s, watermilfoil had also covered thousands of hectares in British Columbia and Ontario, Canada,<ref name=cabi/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Bole|first=J.B.|author2=Allan, J.R.|title=Uptake of Phosphorus from Sediment by Aquatic Plants, Myriophyllum spicatum and Hydrilla verticillata|journal=Water Research|year=1978|volume=12|issue=5|pages=352–358|doi=10.1016/0043-1354(78)90123-9|bibcode=1978WatRe..12..353B }}</ref> and spread some {{convert|500|km|mi}} downstream via the [[Columbia River]] system into the [[Pacific Northwest]] of the United States.<ref name=cabi/>     [[Eurasia]]n watermilfoil is now found across most of Northern America where it is recognized as a noxious weed.<ref>{{cite web|title=Myriophyllum spicatum L.|url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=mysp2|work=Plants Database|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture|access-date=18 December 2012}}</ref>

===Impact===
In lakes or other aquatic areas where native aquatic plants are not well established, the Eurasian watermilfoil plant can spread quickly.<ref name=cabi/> Eurasian watermilfoil has been known to crowd out native plants and create dense mats that interfere with recreational activity.<ref name=cabi/> Dense growth of Eurasian milfoil can also have a negative impact on fisheries by creating microhabitats for juvenile fish and obstructing space for larger fish, ultimately disrupting normal feeding patterns. Due to the Eurasian milfoil plant's inability to provide the same microhabitat for invertebrates created by native aquatic plant species, densely populated areas of Eurasian milfoil create an ecosystem with fewer food sources for the surrounding fish. Dense Eurasian milfoil growth can also create hypoxic zones by blocking out sun penetration to native aquatic vegetation, preventing them from photosynthesizing.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Engel|first=Sandy|date=January 9, 2011|title=Eurasian Watermilfoil as a Fishery Management Tool|journal=Fisheries|volume=20|issue=3|pages=20–27|doi=10.1577/1548-8446(1995)020<0020:EWAAFM>2.0.CO;2}}</ref> Eurasian watermilfoil grows primarily from broken off stems, known as shoot fragments, which increases the rate at which the plant can spread and grow. In some areas, the Eurasian Watermilfoil is an Aquatic Nuisance Species.<ref name=cabi/> Eurasian watermilfoil is known to hybridize with the native northern watermilfoil (''M. sibiricum'') and the hybrid taxon has also become invasive in North America.<ref name=cabi/> This hybridization has been observed across the upper midwestern United States (Indiana, Minnesota, Michigan, Wisconsin) and in the Northwest (Idaho, Washington).<ref>{{cite journal|last=Moody|first=M. L.|author2=Les, D. H.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, USA|year=2002|volume=99|issue=23|pages=14867–14871|doi=10.1073/pnas.172391499|title=Evidence of hybridity in invasive watermilfoil (Myriophyllum) populations|pmc=137510|pmid=12407174|bibcode=2002PNAS...9914867M|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Control and management===
It is impossible to completely eradicate the species once Eurasian watermilfoil is established. As a result, removal must be done to reduce an infestation to levels affordably controlled, with continued maintenance thereafter. Effective management techniques include insect biocontrol and hand-harvesting of the plant.

The [[Aquatic insect|aquatic moth]] ''[[Acentria|Acentria ephemerella]]'', the water veneer moth, feeds upon and damages this water milfoil. It has been used as an agent of [[biological pest control]] against the plant in North America. The milfoil weevil (''[[Euhrychiopsis lecontei]]'') has also been used as biocontrol.

Another method for biocontrol is [[grass carp]], (one of the [[Asian carp]] species) which have been bred as [[Sterility (physiology)|sterile]] and is sometimes released into affected areas. These fish primarily feed on aquatic plants and have proven effective at controlling the spread. However, the carp prefer many native species over the milfoil and will usually devastate preferred species before eating the milfoil. In Washington State the success rate of grass carp has been less than expected, where they were used in 98 lakes, and 39 percent of them had no submerged plant life left after only a short time.<ref>{{cite web|title=Aquatic Plant Management – Triploid Grass Carp |url=http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/wq/plants/management/aqua024.html|publisher=Washington State Department of Ecology|access-date=18 December 2012}}</ref>

Hand-harvesting of invasive milfoils has shown much success as a management technique since around 2000. Several organizations in the New England states have undertaken large scale, lake-wide hand-harvesting management programs with extremely successful results. Well trained divers with proper techniques have been able to effectively control and then maintain many lakes, especially in the Adirondack Park in Northern New York where chemicals, mechanical harvesters, and other disruptive and largely unsuccessful management techniques are banned. After only three years of hand harvesting in Saranac Lake the program was able to reduce the amount harvested from over 18 tons to just 800 pounds per year.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fund Supports Upper Saranac Lake Foundation Efforts|url=http://www.generousact.org/stories/fund-supports-upper-saranac-lake-foundation-efforts|publisher=Adirondack Community Trust|access-date=18 December 2012|archive-date=7 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141107062350/https://www.generousact.org/stories/fund-supports-upper-saranac-lake-foundation-efforts}}</ref>

Raking is not recommended as milfoil will reproduce from the fragments.<ref name=pennstate>{{cite web |title=Eurasian Water Milfoil |publisher=[[Penn State Extension]] |url=https://extension.psu.edu/eurasian-water-milfoil |access-date=26 March 2026}}</ref>  However, raking can be useful for clearing channels.<ref>{{cite web|title=Eurasian watermilfoil control options |publisher=Minnesota Aquatic Invasive Species Research Center (MAISRC) |url=https://extension.psu.edu/eurasian-water-milfoil |access-date=26 March 2026}}</ref>

In order to prevent damages from mass growth of the plant in lakes, the water level can be lowered. By freezing out the bottom of the bank in the winter months, the population of the plant decreases.<ref name=pennstate/><ref>{{cite web|title=So hält man eine Wasserpflanze in Schach |date=17 December 2022 |url=https://www.suedkurier.de/region/hochrhein/uehlingen-birkendorf/so-haelt-man-eine-wasserpflanze-in-schach;art372595,11402029|access-date=17 January 2023}}</ref>

[[ProcellaCOR]], an aquatic herbicide, has also been used to control infestations.

===Spread prevention===
Trailering boats has proven to be a significant vector by which Eurasian milfoil is able to spread and proliferate across otherwise disconnected bodies of water. Effective methods for mitigating this spread include visual inspections with subsequent hand removal and pressure washing upon boat removal.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rothlisberger|first=John|date=January 9, 2011|title=Aquatic Invasive Species Transport via Trailered Boats: What Is Being Moved, Who Is Moving It, and What Can Be Done|journal=Fisheries|volume=35|issue=3|pages=121–132|doi=10.1577/1548-8446-35.3.121}}</ref> In the [[Okanagan Basin|Okanagan River Basin]] of south-central [[British Columbia]], a specially-adapted [[rototiller]] is used to [[dredge]] shallow water to damage or destroy the root system.<ref name="obwb">{{cite web |title=Milfoil |url=https://www.obwb.ca/milfoil/ |publisher=Okanagan Basin Water Board |access-date=4 March 2019 |date=2019}}</ref>
